qt: to the Commission Alessandro Zan (S&D), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Lucia Annunziata (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Stefano Bonaccini (S&D), Pina Picierno (S&D), Elisabetta Gualmini (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Antonio Decaro (S&D), Camilla Laureti (S&D), Irene Tinagli (S&D), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Raffaele Topo (S&D), Dario Nardella (S&D), Matteo Ricci (S&D), Pierfrancesco Maran (S&D) Subject:

On 18 September 2024, the Italian Chamber of Deputies passed the draft law on ‘Provisions on public security’ which amends the criminal code to tighten up existing penalties, introduce new sanctions and establish new criminal offences, including the act of ‘passive resistance’ within penal institutions, punishable with imprisonment, thus aggravating the situation in Italy’s prisons. Provisions punishing ‘passive resistance’ in detention and reception facilities for migrants have also been adopted, together with the obligation for non-EU citizens to provide a copy of their residence permit if they wish to purchase a SIM card. The act of obstructing traffic on roads or railways during demonstrations is also due to be transformed from a misdemeanour worthy of an administrative sanction into a crime punishable with imprisonment. If this is with the intention of preventing public works or the building of strategic infrastructure it will be deemed to be an aggravating circumstance. The mandatory deferral of sentences for pregnant women or mothers with children less than one year old is also to be abolished. In view of these provisions, Article 2 TEU, Articles 11 and 12 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and CJEU case-law, can the Commission say: 1.
Whether it considers these provisions to be in breach of the principles of freedom of expression, assembly and association?
Whether it believes these provisions to undermine the principle of human dignity?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.11.2024) Human dignity, freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and of association are respectively protected by Article 1, Article 11 and Article 12 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (the Charter) and the Commission is committed to ensuring their respect within the remit of its competences. According to its Article 51(1), the Charter applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law. The Italian draft law on ’Provisions on public security’ lays down, inter alia, national provisions introducing criminal offences related to ‘passive resistance’ or obstructing traffic on roads or railways during demonstrations, and the amount of the penalties for these offences. Such provisions do not seem to fall within the scope of the Charter, as they do not implement any EU legislation. The EU competence in the area of substantive criminal law is set out in Article 83 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) and does not cover the areas of crime concerned by the Italian draft law on ‘Provisions on public security’. Furthermore, in accordance with Article 72 TFEU, Member States are responsible for maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security. Therefore, it is for the Member States, including their judicial authorities, to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected, in accordance with their national legislation and international human rights obligations.
